title: Spending on others
hookLine: spending on others lifted happiness more than spending on oneself (Dunn, Aknin and Norton)

lines: ON YOU, OR ON SOMEONE ELSE?
cards: An envelope, a little cash, and a slip of paper with one instruction. On a university campus, researchers handed these to people in the morning. Some slips said: spend this on yourself by five o'clock today.
A bill, a treat, a gift for you. Others said: spend it on someone else, or give it to charity. That evening, each person got a phone call and one question: how happy are you feeling right now?
Before hearing the answer, a guess: which slip sounds like the happier day?

teach.b: First, the study. Psychologists Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton ran that envelope experiment, telling people at random to spend the money on themselves or on others. Second, the result.

In the evening, the people who had spent on others reported feeling happier than the people who had spent on themselves, and how much was in the envelope mattered less than where the money went. Third, the twist.
The researchers asked a separate group to predict the outcome.

Those people mostly guessed the opposite: that spending on yourself would make you happier, and that more money would matter most. Our own forecasts about what will make us glad can be off. Fourth, older voices.
In the Acts of the Apostles, Paul reminds a gathering of the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, in the King James Version: "It is more blessed to give than to receive."

In the Pali texts, when the Buddha gives his step-by-step talk to a newcomer, the first topic is giving, called dana. Two paths, each with its own reasons, each putting giving near the heart of a good life.
The science is smaller and plainer; it just measured a mood at the end of an ordinary day.
But it found the same direction: a little of what you have, spent for someone else, came back that evening as a happier answer on the phone.

how: Giving is a practice in Christianity and Buddhism alike: Christians recall Jesus' words that it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35), and in the Buddha's graduated talk, dana, generosity, is the first topic; some people set aside a small amount each week to spend on others.

o: using a little money for someone else, not yourself
saving money now so you can help people later
paying back a debt you owe to a friend

games.q: inside the envelope study: tap the pairs.

s: in the study, bigger envelopes made the biggest difference
the size mattered less than where the money went.
people asked to predict the result mostly got it right
they mostly guessed spending on yourself would make you happier.
Acts records Paul recalling that it is more blessed to give than to receive
Paul reminds a gathering of those words of the Lord Jesus in Acts 20:35.

games.q: you're handed an envelope of cash to spend by five. which spending did the study link to more happiness by evening?
games.why: people who spent on others reported feeling happier that evening, even though most predictions said the opposite.

practice: Bring three people to mind, someone close, someone at work or school, someone you barely know, and for each picture one small thing you could get them: a coffee, a pastry, a flower, a bus fare, a donation in their name.
Choose one, see yourself handing it over, and notice what happens in your chest.

wordCard.voice: Spending on others. In one study, people told to spend a little money on someone else ended the day happier than those who spent it on themselves. Today's word.

orig.note: dana: giving or generosity, in Pali and Sanskrit, the first topic of the Buddha's graduated talk.

carryVoice: Your line: for someone else. The size of the gift matters less than where it goes. See you in the morning.

sources.ref: Dunn, Aknin and Norton, "Spending money on others promotes happiness" (Science)

sources.q: It is more blessed to give than to receive.

sources.ref: dana (giving) in Buddhist teaching, e.g. the graduated talk (anupubbi-katha) that begins with giving
